Title: The White Elephant MC: Comedy, Control & Modeling Walks

Quick answer
The Master of Ceremonies is the person who runs a white elephant exchange like a show: coordinating whose turn it is, spotlighting each gift as it is revealed, ruling on disputes, and generating the comedy. Without one, the game becomes a rules argument with a room attached. This page is the MC playbook.
## Why the game needs one
Left unmanaged, a white elephant is a rules question with a room attached: Who's next? Can she steal that? Is that gift locked? Can he DO that? The Master of Ceremonies answers all of it in character — coordinating the action, calling attention to each gift as it's revealed, ruling on disputes with instant fake-judicial authority, and generating the comedy that separates a great exchange from a board-game-night argument. Every legendary game you've ever heard about (see the steal-chain archive) had one. Every family law in existence was read aloud by one (the Aunt Karen Addendum needs a voice). The MC is why the youngest participant's near-tears moment becomes a story instead of a disaster.
## The five jobs
### Coordinate the action
Read the rules aloud before the game. Call turn numbers with ceremony ("Number seven — approach the pile"). Track the Three-Owner Rule lock count publicly, because the room will absolutely disagree about it. Manage steal chains so the game never stalls: "The gift is locked — pick your poison, open or steal elsewhere."
### Call attention to the gift
Every unwrap is a product launch. Hold it up. Read any absurd packaging. Give the reveal a drumroll when the room wants one. The MC's hype is the difference between "oh, a candle" and "BEHOLD: a candle — its half-used predecessor fetched more steals than a television."
### Create comedy
Interview the stealers ("Why her? Why today?"). Award superlatives. Demand the modeling walk for ridiculous wearables — see the bits below. The MC doesn't have to be funny; the MC just has to hold the microphone close to the people who are.
### Guard the vulnerable
The youngest participant is always at risk to cry when their favorite gift is taken — the MC watches them all game, cues the consolation bowl, and enforces the protections. At senior gatherings, the MC delivers gifts to laps and calls every steal slowly and kindly.
### Enforce the law
House rules read aloud like a court convening. Collusive steal-and-lock schemes voided on discovery, with the name of the ruling cited ("That's Karen-level coordination — void!"). Player 1's final swap announced with full gravity. The gavel is optional. The bias for drama is not.
## The comedy bits (a starter kit)
### The Modeling Walk
Signature move · use 1–2× per party
The crown jewel. When a wearable or ridiculous gift is revealed — enormous fleece, onesie pajamas, a hat shaped like a mistake — the MC asks the new owner to model their new gift: one lap around the room, catwalk rules, music if available. Declining costs a steal token (a house rule in many families); performing earns permanent standing. And when a wearable gift is stolen, the rule follows the gift: the thief wears it — the walk happens on the spot, mid-celebration, in front of the person they robbed. Never force it more than twice a party — the walk is comedy because it's voluntary-ish.
### The Steal Interrogation
After any steal
Microphone to the stealer: "State your name and your reasoning." The answers — "it matches my kitchen," "revenge," "look at it" — are funnier than anything scripted. Tween-tier interrogations produce the best material of all.
### The Infomercial
When an As-Seen-on-TV gift appears
The MC narrates a full fake ad for the gift just revealed: "Are YOU tired of avocados ripening on THEIR schedule?" The room joins by the second sentence. Pairs perfectly with the As Seen on TV theme.
### The Lock Ceremony
When a gift hits its third owner
The MC freezes the moment with the gift: "This gift has known three owners. It has known betrayal. It is LOCKED." Holder poses with the gift. One photograph. It will be shown at every future gathering.
### The Weather Report
Mid-game, big rooms
"Here's the steal forecast: heavy chains in the northeast corner, a 90% chance the blanket moves again, and Aunt Diane remains an island." Play-by-play of the room as if it's a storm system. Works best at 20+ players.
## Casting the MC
The best MCs are not the funniest people in the family — they're the most fearless: the one who'll hold silence for a drumroll, sing the infomercial, and void Aunt Karen's scheme to her face with a straight voice. Rotate annually if tradition demands it, but many families find their MC the way they find their Thanksgiving turkey recipe: by conquest. Brief them on the rulebook, arm them with the house laws, and hand them the aux cord.
## Appoint your MC. Then give them rules worth announcing.
The full rulebook — Three-Owner Rule, steal-backs, Player 1's final swap — is the MC's script.
Read the rules →
## MC FAQ
What does a white elephant MC actually do?
Coordinates turn order and steal chains, narrates every gift reveal, produces the comedy (modeling walks, interrogations, infomercials), guards the youngest players, and enforces the house rules with fake-judicial authority.
What is the modeling walk?
The MC's signature bit: the new owner of a ridiculous wearable gift takes one lap around the room with it on. Declining costs a steal token; performing earns eternal respect. Codified in many families as the Marquee Rule.
Does the modeling walk apply to stolen gifts?
Yes — the rule follows the gift, not the reveal. When a wearable is stolen, the thief wears it: the walk happens on the spot, mid-celebration, in front of the player they just robbed. Declining still costs a steal token, and the person they stole it from is invited to judge the fit.
Does the MC play too?
They can — many do, holding their gift while working the room. For big games (20+), a dedicated non-playing MC keeps the pace up and the drama fair.
What if nobody wants to be MC?
The host drafted themselves the moment they sent the invite. Second choice: last year's most enthusiastic stealer. Third: whomever laughs loudest — proximity to the microphone does the rest.
How does the MC handle a crying kid?
Immediately and without ceremony: consolation bowl, a chair next to a non-stealer, and a promise (kept) that the next number drawn will be theirs. The age-group guide has the full tear-proofing setup.

Title: White Elephant FAQ: Every Question, Answered

Quick answer
This FAQ answers the most-argued white elephant questions: how many times a gift can be stolen, whether you can steal back immediately, what Player 1's final swap is, what to do if you hate your gift, how it differs from Yankee Swap, plus budgets, kids, themes, and the Lookback Rule.
## The basics
What is a white elephant gift exchange?
A party game where every guest brings one wrapped gift to a shared pile. Players take numbered turns either unwrapping a new gift or stealing an opened one. Under the standard Three-Owner Rule, a gift locks once it has had three owners, and Player 1 gets a final swap after the last gift is unwrapped. Full walkthrough: the rulebook.
Why is it called a white elephant?
From the legend of the King of Siam gifting ruinous albino elephants to courtiers he disliked, and the English idiom for a burdensome possession. Historians dispute the legend; the idiom is real. Honest origin story on the homepage.
How many people do you need?
Five to fifty. Under five, just swap gifts; over twenty-five, split into circles or use speed caps — the office guide covers big-group logistics.
How long does a game take?
Roughly two minutes per player with the Three-Owner Rule: a 12-person game runs 25–30 minutes. Timer-based game modes guarantee a hard stop.
What do I do if I hate my white elephant gift?
It happens to one player almost every game — Uncle Randall's Dollar Store find from 2016 included. Gracious fixes: ask the giver to donate it (or send it to Aunt Edna, who liked it at the reveal), redirect an un-ordered retailer gift ('Hey, Venmo me and I'll buy it here' or 'Could you donate what you would have spent to the following charity?'), regift it under the Legend Returns Clause, or trade quietly after the game. No hard feelings — one person's trash is another person's treasure, and vice versa.
## Rules & disputes
How many times can a gift be stolen?
Under the standard Three-Owner Rule, a gift locks after three owners — the original opener plus two steals. Two-owner caps speed up big games; Cutthroat Christmas variants allow unlimited steals with a timer. Full rulebook.
Can you steal your gift back immediately?
No — the standard rules ban immediate steal-backs. The player who was just robbed must unwrap a new gift or steal a different one.
Does the first player get to steal at the end?
Yes. Once the last unopened gift is unwrapped, Player 1 gets one final swap with any unlocked gift — which can trigger one final steal chain.
What happens when your gift is stolen?
You immediately take a new turn: unwrap from the pile or steal from someone else. No one is ever left giftless mid-game.
Is a collusive steal-and-lock scheme legal?
Not under the Aunt Karen Addendum — pre-arranged steal deals between players are voided on discovery, and permanently cited as "Karen-level coordination." The full statute book: family house rules.
## Names & regions
What is another name for the game?
Yankee Swap (New England), Dirty Santa (the American South), Pollyanna (PA/NJ, where it often means a Secret Santa–style draw), and Rob Your Neighbor (the Midwest) — plus Thieving Elves, Shifty Santa, the Grinch Game, Cutthroat Christmas, and more. Complete glossary: every name, mapped.
Are Yankee Swap and white elephant the same game?
Mechanically yes. Yankee Swaps traditionally lean toward desirable gifts; white elephant pools traditionally lean gag. Yankee Swap vs. Dirty Santa, compared.
## Gifts
What makes a good white elephant gift?
Gifts fall into five types: cultural zeitgeist items, Christmas classics, useful house items, booze and scratch-offs, and gift certificates to a local haunt — plus exactly one wildcard legend per party. The taxonomy: the five gift types.
What gift gets stolen the most?
The booze-and-scratchers category leads reported steal counts — a bottle of Bailey's was once stolen six-plus times in a single game — with zeitgeist items close behind. The full hall of fame: best gift ideas.
What budget should I set?
$20 is the family classic, $25–$50 the office norm, $10–$15 for kids' parties. The cap matters more than the number — publish it in the invite with the gift tone. Budget tables: office guide.
What should I NOT bring?
Worn regifts, body-size-dependent items, heavy scents, perishables that can't survive the party, and personal roast gifts at work. The graveyard list: gift ideas page.
Can a past winning gift come back another year?
Yes — under the Legend Returns Clause, favorite gifts may reappear the next year, or two, or five years later. The current holder hides the real gift elsewhere in the house and re-wraps a small, unassuming box containing only a clue card — "Go into the Pantry for your gift." The unwrap becomes a treasure-hunt reveal, and the room spends the rest of the night wondering what else the host hid. Full statute: the Legend Returns Clause.
How does a hidden redeployed gift work during the game?
When the decoy box is unwrapped, the MC reads the card aloud, the owner leaves the circle on the quest, and the game pauses for the reveal — the most dramatic non-steal moment in the sport. Capped only by the host's real estate.
I haven't found a gift yet — can I still play?
Yes. When you add your gift, just paste a link from an online retailer — Amazon, Target, Walmart, wherever you shop — and it becomes your gift in the pile. No wrapping, no shipping panic, no explaining yourself to the host. Shippers of last-minute gifts, rejoice.
## Formats, ages & hosting
Can kids play white elephant?
Yes — one steal per gift, a themed pool, a consolation bowl for stolen-from kids, and an MC watching the youngest players. The youngest participant is always at risk to cry when a favorite gift is taken; the tear-proof setup: age-group guide.
How do you run one at a senior center?
Seated circle, easy-open wrapping, slow-loud narration, generous steal caps, and the Zero Forced Steals courtesy — nobody has to take a gift from anyone. Senior-center section.
What does the Master of Ceremonies do?
Coordinates turn order and steal chains, narrates every gift, enforces house law, guards the youngest players, and runs the comedy — including the modeling walk, which applies to stolen gifts too: the thief wears it. Full playbook: the MC guide.
What are the best game variations?
Dice Roll Chaos (a die roll replaces your choice), Mystery Bag (nothing opens until the end), the Hot Potato timer, Regift-Only, and the Left-Right story game. Full rules per mode: game modes.
What is the Lookback Rule?
Before the game begins, the MC reviews the last three years' most-stolen gifts and reigning champions aloud, so the whole room sees what was chosen recently. It prevents accidental duplicates, briefs new members on the family's steal history, and takes about ninety seconds. Duplicates are taxed one consolation-bowl candy. Full statute: the Lookback Rule.
Should I theme my exchange?
Themes fix the gag-vs-serious expectation problem in one word — try Regift Chaos, Dollar Store Mayhem, or Keep It Local. Fifteen themes with invite wording: party themes.
## Question not answered here?
Every answer above links its deep dive — the rulebook alone settles 90% of disputes. For the other 10%, there's the amendment process.
Read the rulebook →

- Mental Floss: Rules and Origins of 6 Gift Exchanges: Regional names and the folklore behind Yankee Swap and Dirty Santa.

## Gag & Games
The chaos wing. Objects of pure charisma — the gifts that start steal chains and end silent nights.
### Codenames 2025 Edition

## How a premium gift warps the game
Money changes the math. Run it on purpose, not by accident.
Under the Three-Owner Rule, a luxury lip balm will hit its three owners in the first three turns — it is the de facto trophy, so the Master of Ceremonies should call it out loud when it unwraps. If the pile splits cheap-gag versus premium, consider announcing a house amendment before Player 1 goes: a premium-tier second swap, or a no-touch first pass for anything over $50. In a Yankee Swap, premium gifts are exactly why the final-swap rule exists — the last player should get one honest shot at the French press.
## Premium gift FAQ
The questions that come up when someone puts a luxury lip balm on the table.
How much should a premium white elephant gift cost?
Most parties set a $20–$25 limit; $30–$100 is the generous tier. If you are spending that much, you are either independently wealthy or you really love this group — both are legal, but announce the budget break to the host first.
Is it fair to bring an expensive gift to a white elephant?
It is allowed unless your host caps the price. Expect it to be stolen to its three-owner limit immediately, which is either the point or the problem.
What is the best $30–$100 white elephant gift?
A steal magnet with broad appeal: the Frieling French press for caffeine people, Magical Athlete for game people, a wooden Artifact puzzle for quiet people, and La Mer lip balm for anyone who wants to watch the room react.
Should expensive gifts get their own rules?
Some houses add a premium tier — a second swap round or a no-touch first pass. Hand the call to your Master of Ceremonies and announce it before Player 1 unwraps.

Title: Virtual White Elephant: Play Online or Async

Quick answer
A virtual white elephant uses the same rules online: players draw numbers, unwrap or steal, and the Three-Owner Rule locks gifts. You can play live on video, spread turns across a week, or follow along from anywhere. Stolen Elephants holds the turn order and tracks every steal and lock automatically.
One pile, three speeds: play live on a video call with the app keeping the order, play async so each teammate takes their turn inside their own workday, or flip on spectator-plus so anyone following along can still be pulled into the steal chain. Same gifts, same drama, zero conference-room booking. No gift yet? No panic. When you add your gift, just paste a link from an online retailer — Amazon, Target, or anywhere else — and the app turns it into a proper pile entry. Your recipient gets a direct link to their winning loot, not a mystery box they have to guess about.
## Three ways to play from the same pile
Pick a speed per event. Switch mid-game if someone's flight gets in.
### Live on Video
LIVE
Everyone on Zoom, Meet, or Teams; the app holds the turn order so nobody has to be the person who says 'whose turn is it?' ever again.
The classic party, broadcast. The host draws numbers in the app, shares the screen, and every steal, lock, and final swap is tracked in real time.
See the rules it enforces →
### Async Across the Week
ASYNC
Turns happen between standups, school pickups, and time zones. The drama arrives as push notifications instead of screams.
Open the event Monday; each player unwraps or steals on their own clock. The app polices the Three-Owner Rule so an async steal is just as binding as a live one.
How async fits a work week →
### Spectator-Plus
SPECTATE
For the teammate on a plane, in a hospital chair, or holding a newborn. They watch every steal land — and can still steal when their turn comes.
Follow the action steal by steal from any browser, and participate for real: remote players take genuine turns, never a proxy gif and a sorry.
Where it matters most →
## How a virtual game runs, start to finish
Five steps. The host does about ten minutes of work total.
- Create the event — set the mode (live, async, or hybrid), the price cap, and any house amendments.
- Invite the link — one URL joins from phone or laptop, no app store detour. Dispersed team, distant cousins: same link.
- The app draws numbers — order is public and final, which kills 90% of pre-game conspiracy theories.
- Turns fire in sequence — unwrap or steal; the software enforces the Three-Owner Rule, blocks immediate steal-backs, and runs the final swap automatically.
- Everyone leaves with a gift — and the receipts to prove whose Grinch hands touched it last.
## The rules don't change — the room does
Software referees better than a cousin with a beer.
A virtual game is still a white elephant: three owners and a gift locks, no immediate steal-backs, and Player 1's final swap when the last gift opens. The difference is that the app — not a Master of Ceremonies — tracks every lock, which is exactly what you want when half the room is on mute. Async games get a short turn window per player so one distracted uncle can't stall the chain across a long weekend.
## Virtual White Elephant FAQ
The questions that come up before the first steal.
Can you play white elephant virtually with people in different time zones?
Yes. Run it async: the event stays open across days, each player takes their turn when their day allows, and the app enforces the same Three-Owner Rule and steal-back bans as a live game.
How does an async white elephant work?
Players are notified when it's their turn, unwrap or steal from the shared pile, and the next player is prompted automatically. A week-long game fits every team's calendar without a single meeting invite.
Can someone join a white elephant from a hospital or airport?
Yes — spectator-plus mode lets anyone follow the action live and take real turns from a phone browser. Remote players are participants, not afterthoughts.
Do virtual games work for Yankee Swap too?
Yes. The Yankee Swap final-swap sequence runs the same way: the app tracks owners and executes the last-player swap without a vote count on a whiteboard.
## Host your first virtual game free
Up to 8 players costs nothing. Bigger crowd — or a whole distributed company — runs $19 to $99 per event. The FAQ covers the rest.

Title: Remote Team White Elephant: Async Team Building

Quick answer
A remote team can run a white elephant over a week instead of a single meeting. The host posts one event link, each player is pinged when it's their turn, and unwraps and steals happen between meetings, about fifteen minutes per person. Pick the budget first; $20 is the office standard.
The pitch to your people team: team building without the trust falls — and with double the laughter. Nobody has to disclose a childhood fear on a whiteboard; they just have to defend a desk waffle maker from a colleague two oceans away. No gift yet? No panic. When you add your gift, just paste a link from an online retailer — Amazon, Target, or anywhere else — and the app turns it into a proper pile entry. Your recipient gets a direct link to their winning loot, not a mystery box they have to guess about.
## A week-long game that fits the workday
Fifteen minutes per person, spread across the week. Zero calendar invites.
### Monday: open the pile
DAY 1
The host posts the event link in Slack. Players peek at nothing — the pile is sealed — and get their draw order.
Set the budget cap ($20 is the office standard), paste the link, done. Even the async-averse can handle it in a coffee break.
Pick the budget first →
### Tuesday–Thursday: turns land
DAYS 2–4
Each player gets pinged when it's their turn. Unwraps and steals happen between standups; the steal chain updates live for everyone watching.
This is where the async magic shows up: the person in Lisbon wakes up to find their gift was stolen by the person in Seattle at 6 p.m. Pacific. Fully legal. Fully tracked.
How async enforcement works →
### Friday: the final steal chain
FINALE
Last gift opens, Player 1 gets the final swap, and the whole company watches the chain resolve. Best 15 minutes of the week, guaranteed.
Book one optional 15-minute call for the finale — or let it close async and read the chaos in the event log Monday morning.
See the final-swap rule →
## Why distributed teams get more out of it than co-located ones
The gift pile becomes the water cooler.
Co-located offices have the break room; remote teams have notifications. An async white elephant manufactures the small, harmless drama — who stole the good candles? — that distributed teams otherwise never get. It works for hybrid squads too: the folks in the conference room and the folks on the screen see the same board, and nobody in either group is a second-class player.
It also scales with the org chart: a team of 8 plays free, a department of 40 runs $19 per event, and a whole-company brawl up to 150 players is $99 — the same pricing as every Stolen Elephants event.
## Keep it classy enough for the all-hands
A quick word from your friendly HR partner.
The office edition has its own etiquette — budget caps, no procedural-gift recycling, and a dedicated playbook. For a distributed team, add two: announce the house rules in writing before Monday, and let the app's MC functions make the controversial calls, because 'the software decided' ends debates that a manager can't.
## Remote Team White Elephant FAQ
The questions that come up before the first steal.
How do you do a white elephant with a remote team?
Create an async event, share one join link, and let each person take their turn during their own workday. The app tracks turn order, steals, and locks — no meeting required, though an optional finale call is fun.
How long should an async work white elephant run?
Three to five business days is the sweet spot: enough time for every player to take a turn without being chased, short enough that the pile still feels alive on finale day.
What price cap works for a remote team gift exchange?
$20 is the office norm; some teams do $30 for a 'premium' year. Announce the cap with the invite so nobody shows up with a luxury lip balm against a $20 pile — or everyone does, and the steal chain gets legendary.
Is a virtual gift exchange good team building for hybrid teams?
Yes — in-room and remote players share one board, one order, and one steal chain, so neither group becomes the second-class audience of a conference-room-only party.

Title: Play White Elephant From Anywhere: Hospital to Airport

Quick answer
Anyone can take a real turn in a white elephant game from a phone, from anywhere. Stolen Elephants lets players follow every steal live and still unwrap or steal on their turn, built for situations like a hospital stay, an airport layover, or a time-zone gap, so no one is left watching as a spectator.
The whole point: being far away is not the same as being less present. A spectator-plus player sees every unwrap and every steal as it happens, and when their number comes up, they choose — steal the candle or unwrap the mystery. No proxy decisions, no 'we saved you the leftovers.' No gift yet? No panic. When you add your gift, just paste a link from an online retailer — Amazon, Target, or anywhere else — and the app turns it into a proper pile entry. Your recipient gets a direct link to their winning loot, not a mystery box they have to guess about.
## Where this mode earns its keep
The four situations we built it for.
### The hospital stay
BEDSIDE
Grandma's recovering on the 4th floor but she is NOT missing the exchange. She follows each steal on her phone and steals the blanket from her hospital bed with full authority.
Wi-fi and one hand free is the only equipment required. The family plays around her; she plays with them.
Family setups like this →
### The airport purgatory
LAYOVER
Stranded in Dallas with a three-hour delay? Take your turn from gate B12. Steal, unwrap, gloat, board the plane.
Turns are short on purpose: a minute on your phone is a complete turn, and the pile moves on without waiting for your boarding call.
How async turns work →
### The overseas posting
GMT+7
Stationed abroad or backpacking through a different hemisphere? The event's clock bends to your calendar, not the family's kitchen.
Async mode means the difference between your turn landing at 3 a.m. and landing at your 3 p.m. Either way, it's your turn — not your proxy's.
Time-zone play for teams →
### The new-parent year
NAPTIME
Baby's asleep on exactly the wrong schedule. Play from the nursery during the 2 a.m. feed — the one party you can attend in a rocking chair.
Spectator-plus was designed for the person who can't leave the house and can't miss the game. Same turns, same steals, same bragging rights.
More family rules →
## Follow the action steal by steal
Not a scoreboard. The actual drama.
A spectator-plus player gets the live event view: the pile, the turn order, every unwrap revealed as it happens, every steal chain as it resolves. Push notifications flag when it's their turn — and when the Three-Owner Rule locks the gift they had their eye on. It's the difference between watching the game and being in it, and it works for a Yankee Swap exactly the same way.
## White Elephant From Anywhere FAQ
The questions that come up before the first steal.
Can someone in a hospital play a white elephant remotely?
Yes. They join from a phone browser, follow every steal live, and take their real turn when their number comes up — no proxy, no exceptions made on their behalf.
What if my turn comes while I'm on a plane or asleep?
In async mode the event waits for you within the host's turn window. Hosts can keep a strict cadence or let the game breathe across days; the pile and rules are identical either way.
Do remote players get ignored in virtual gift exchanges?
Not in this one. Spectator-plus exists so distant players see the same drama in real time and act on it — the design goal was exactly that nobody becomes an afterthought.
Can a player join late from another country?
Yes. The join link works from any browser, and a late arrival slots into the draw order the app has already published. Time zones are handled by async turns, not by asking twelve relatives to wake up early.

Title: Long-Distance Family White Elephant & Yankee Swap

Quick answer
A long-distance family can keep its white elephant tradition with one shared pile. Pick a week instead of a day so each household plays on its own schedule; everyone ships a gift ahead; the app draws the order and tracks the steals; and the Three-Owner Rule ends disputes over how many times a gift moved.
The tradition, minus the travel: no flight required, no kitchen big enough for 22 people, no coordinating whose basement hosts. The pile lives in the app; the family lives wherever life put them; the screaming happens in the group chat. No gift yet? No panic. When you add your gift, just paste a link from an online retailer — Amazon, Target, or anywhere else — and the app turns it into a proper pile entry. Your recipient gets a direct link to their winning loot, not a mystery box they have to guess about.
## How the family game runs across the map
Same skeleton as the kitchen-table classic, stretched to fit a map.
- Pick the week, not the day. Async events let each household take their turn when the kids are down and the timezone cooperates.
- Ship the gifts ahead. Wrap prices, not presents: everyone buys online and sends directly, or drops one gift at a designated shipper. The app tracks the pile; USPS tracks the boxes.
- The app draws the order. Grandkids first, grandpa last — or however your house amendments run it. Nobody argues with an app at Thanksgiving anymore.
- Turns fire, steals land, locks lock. The Three-Owner Rule ends the 'that's the FOURTH time this gift moved' dispute before it starts.
- The finale call is optional. One short video call for the last unwrap and Player 1's final swap — or skip it and read the chaos in the group chat.
## Every branch of the tree gets a real turn
The people who used to just get a phone call afterward.
### The hospitalized grandparent
BEDSIDE
Follows every steal from a hospital bed and steals the throw blanket back with the full force of matriarchal authority. Attendance: 100%.
Spectator-plus makes the matriarch a player, not a get-well-card recipient.
The anywhere mode →
### The expat sibling
GMT+1
Amsterdam, Dubai, wherever the career went. Their turn lands in their afternoon, not the family's midnight.
Async turns mean 'Merry 3 a.m. Christmas' becomes a scheduling suggestion, not a requirement.
Async, explained →
### The military family
DEPLOYED
Deployment doesn't pause the family tradition. A secure browser and a turn window are all the connection required.
The app's order and locks hold no matter where the player is when their turn arrives.
Rules that travel →
### The new-baby household
NAPTIME
They can't fly with a six-week-old, and nobody wants them to. They play from the nursery and steal at 2 a.m.
The youngest player in the game doesn't have to attend; the Youngest Player Protection Act protects them anyway.
Family house rules →
## The Yankee Swap version, for the purists
Same pile, different finale.
Families that play strict Yankee Swap — every gift owned by exactly one person at once, final swap for Player 1 — get the identical treatment virtually. The app tracks gift ownership through every steal and runs the last-player swap without anyone counting on their fingers. Async or live, the swap sequence is the same drama with a longer fuse.
## Long Distance Family White Elephant FAQ
The questions that come up before the first steal.
How do we do a family white elephant when everyone lives far apart?
Run an async event: gifts ship directly to recipients, each household takes a turn during its own week, and the app tracks every steal and lock. One finale video call is optional.
Can a family member in the hospital participate?
Yes — spectator-plus mode lets them follow every steal live and take their real turns from a phone. The game comes to the bedside instead of waiting for the discharge.
Do gifts have to be shipped before the game starts?
Best practice, yes: buy online and ship directly, so the winner's prize is already en route when they unwrap. The pile is tracked in the app either way.
Does the Three-Owner Rule still work asynchronously?
Yes — the app enforces it in real time regardless of when each player takes their turn. Async steals lock gifts exactly like live ones, no honor system required.
## Keep the tradition running this year
Family-sized events beyond 8 players run $19 (Party, 9–40) — cheaper than one airport lunch. Full rules live in the FAQ.

Title: Virtual White Elephant No-No's: Gifts That Can't Ship

Quick answer
In a virtual white elephant, every gift has to survive shipping. Avoid alcohol and anything age-restricted, since some states ban direct-to-consumer shipments, and avoid heavy items where the shipping cost outweighs the gift. This page lists the five shipping no-no's, each with a ship-safe swap.
Affiliate disclosure: Some links on this page are shopping links. If you buy through them we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes which gifts we recommend.
When the party moves online, the moving truck joins it. In a virtual white elephant, gifts ship from retailers to winners across states, climates, and customs zones — which quietly disqualifies a few beloved gift categories. Plus, the usual disclaimer for any shoppable list: items can change in price or availability, and some can’t be shipped to specific locations at all (out of the country, Alaska, Hawaii — the classics). No gift yet? No panic. When you add your gift, just paste a link from an online retailer — Amazon, Target, or anywhere else — and the app turns it into a proper pile entry. Your recipient gets a direct link to their winning loot, not a mystery box they have to guess about.
## The five shipping no-no’s
Beloved at the kitchen table, disqualified in the mail. Each card has a ship-safe swap.
### Booze & anything age-restricted
STATE BAN
The Bailey's steal is a live-game legend — online, it's a legal puzzle. Several states ban or restrict direct-to-consumer alcohol shipments, so a liquor link may simply not deliver.
Liquor, wine, and beer can't be shipped to specific states under state law, and many retailers restrict it further. What unwraps fine in Texas may be undeliverable in Utah. Check the destination before you paste the link.
Ship-safe swap: fancy mocktail kit
### The heavy stuff
SHIPPING $$
A cast-iron Dutch oven is a legendary steal — until you see the shipping line on the receipt and the gift budget is gone before the gift begins.
Heavy items (cast iron, small appliances, solid-wood serving boards) can blow your budget with the shipping cost alone — sometimes doubling it. Weight is priced by zone: the farther it flies, the more it costs.
Ship-safe swap: a gift card instead
### Fragile items
BREAKAGE RISK
Hand-blown glass arrives as a bag of shards and a refund form. The steal chain deserves a gift that survives the journey.
Ceramics, glassware, and delicate décor are iffy to send: carrier sorting is not gentle, and 'arrived broken' turns the game's trophy into a claim ticket. If it needs a fortress of bubble wrap, gift the link to something sturdier.
Ship-safe swap: wooden desk toys
### Food & heat/cold-sensitive stuff
MELT/FREEZE
Chocolate in a Phoenix July or candles in a Minnesota January arrive as modern art. Climate is a shipping variable, not a detail.
Food stuffs shipped into extremely hot or cold climates have a rough trip: chocolate melts, candles freeze and crack, wax products sweat, and anything with cocoa butter arrives pre-marbled. Season and destination matter as much as the item.
Ship-safe swap: shelf-stable snacks box
### Lithium-ion battery devices
GROUND ONLY
Power banks and e-toys with big batteries ride the truck, not the plane — ground-only shipping means a slower, stricter trip than the game's finale.
Items with lithium-ion batteries need special care and are normally shipped ground-only: spare batteries and high-capacity packs face air-transport restrictions, and some carriers won't move them at all. Budget the extra days into an async game.
Ship-safe swap: plug-in (no battery) gadgets
## The fine print that saves friendships
Links are promises; retailers are reality.
Any gift link is a snapshot of a moment: items might change their price or availability, or might not be shippable to a specific location — out of the country, Alaska, Hawaii, P.O. boxes, and APO addresses are the usual suspects. A $42 griddle can be $61 by finale day; a “in stock” cushion can be back-ordered to March; a perfectly legal candle kit may simply refuse to check out to an APO box. None of this breaks the game — it just means the smart move is to order late and confirm early.
## The end-of-game trick: order direct, ship once
The Stolen Elephants move that sidesteps most of this list.
Instead of every player shipping their gift cross-country the day they add it, Stolen Elephants allows ordering directly at the end of the game — to participants, so the retailer fulfills the order from its own warehouse. The winner’s real address is known before anything buys a stamp, the retailer ships from the distribution center nearest them, and you can potentially save on shipping versus re-shipping the same box across the country — or rescuing a link that turned out not to ship to Alaska at all. It also keeps every price honest: you pay what the item costs on finale day, not what it cost when you pasted the link.
Pair it with the virtual and async game modes: play the week out, resolve the steal chain, and the final orders go in with real addresses attached. The drama is digital; the packages are practical.
## Virtual no-no’s FAQ
The questions the shipping-truck edition always raises.
Why can't some gifts be shipped in a virtual white elephant?
Four big reasons: state laws ban shipping liquor (and some other goods) to specific states, heavy items can cost more to ship than the gift is worth, fragile items break in transit, and climate-sensitive items like chocolate or candles melt or freeze en route.
Can we gift alcohol in an online gift exchange?
Generally no — liquor can't be shipped to specific states under state law, and most retailers restrict direct-to-consumer alcohol anyway. Pick an age-friendly stand-in unless you know the destination state allows it and the retailer ships there.
Why are lithium battery gifts a problem to ship?
Lithium-ion batteries are a fire risk in the air, so they're normally shipped ground-only with carrier restrictions. That means slower delivery and, for spare or high-capacity packs, limits on whether they move at all.
What if a gift's price or availability changes after the game?
Retail items can change price, go out of stock, or become unshippable to a specific location — Alaska, Hawaii, and out-of-country addresses are the classic cases. That's why Stolen Elephants orders at the end of the game, when the winner's actual address is known, instead of locking in a link days earlier.
## Planning the online game itself?
The virtual white elephant guide covers live, async, and spectator-plus play — the rules run the same from a couch, a hospital bed, or gate B12.

Title: Hate Your White Elephant Gift? 5 Gracious Fixes

Quick answer
If you hate your white elephant gift, you have five options, from kindest to boldest. The gentlest is asking the giver if they'd like to donate it instead; most people are relieved, not offended. Others include passing it to a relative who liked it and offering to buy the item yourself.
First, the truth: this happens to one person almost every game. Somebody ends up with Uncle Randall’s Dollar Store find from 2016, the candle that smells like a dentist’s office, or the mug that says #1 Boss in a font from a gas station. The game’s structure already softens the blow — the Three-Owner Rule caps how many times you can be victimized, and Player 1’s final swap exists partly for this moment. What follows is what to do when it still lands on you.
## Five fixes, from kindest to boldest
Real-world options. Pick the one that matches your family’s temperature.
### Ask the giver to donate it
PHYSICAL GIFT
The kindest sentence in the sport: 'Would you mind if we donated it?' Nine givers out of ten say yes before you finish the question.
If it's a physical gift and you genuinely won't use it, simply ask the giver if they'd like to donate it somewhere instead — most people are relieved, not offended. Bonus route: send it to Aunt Edna, because she seemed to really like it when it was revealed. One person's trash is another person's treasure, and Edna has already claimed this one.
### The Venmo redirect
UNORDERED GIFT
'Hey, Venmo me and I'll buy it here.' Five words that turn a dud into exactly what you wanted, at the same price, with zero feelings harmed.
If the gift could be ordered from a retailer and hasn't been purchased yet, the recipient can say: 'Hey, Venmo me and I'll buy it here' — same budget, your choice of color, size, or model. Works best when the game is async or the order hasn't gone in yet; check the app's end-of-game ordering so the redirect lands before the retailer ships.
### The charity redirect
GIVE-WHERE
'Could you donate what you would have spent to the following charity?' Suddenly the worst gift of the night is someone's best news of the week.
Same setup as the Venmo redirect, different destination: 'Could you donate what you would have spent to the following charity?' You name the cause, they still gave a gift, and nobody's budget changes. It's the classiest steal-back in the modern game — the gift becomes a donation in everyone's name.
### Regift it next year
LEGEND RETURNS
Every family has the travelling fruitcake. Under the Legend Returns Clause, yours can become next year's most feared unwrap.
Formally regift: keep it wrapped (or re-wrap it), store it with the decorations, and deploy it under the Legend Returns Clause next year. House rules govern — some families require the regift to change houses, which keeps the story alive and the target fair.
### Trade quietly after the game
SIDE DEAL
Half the great trades in history happen in the driveway. Find the person who wanted your dud and swap — the app's ownership log makes it official.
After the final swap, find the one person who said 'wait, I actually wanted that' and trade. The game record shows the official winners; the driveway trade is between friends. This is also where 'one person's trash is another person's treasure' does its real work — the pile sorts people perfectly.
## The spirit of the thing
Why none of these moves counts as an insult.
The white elephant deal has always been: one wrapped surprise, zero vetting, and the pile decides. Everyone agrees to that when they draw a number — so being disappointed isn’t a betrayal, and fixing it quietly isn’t a rejection. One person’s trash is another person’s treasure, and vice versa. The Aunt Edna option exists because she genuinely wanted that ceramic lighthouse; the charity redirect exists because the budget was already given. None of the five fixes costs the giver pride or the recipient money — and done with a smile, there are never hard feelings. (And if you gave the dud: laugh, take the Venmo, and enjoy your new status as a cautionary tale. It’s the cheapest tuition in the game.)
Virtual games make this even easier: with order-at-end-of-game, a dud link can be redirected before the retailer ever ships — the Venmo and charity options were practically invented for it.
## “What if I hate my gift?” FAQ
The consolation-prize questions, answered with grace.
What do I do if I hate my white elephant gift?
It happens to one player almost every game — and there are gracious fixes: ask the giver to donate it, redirect an unopened order ('Venmo me and I'll buy it here'), redirect the spend to a charity, regift it next year, or trade quietly after the game. There are never hard feelings; one person's trash is another person's treasure.
Is it rude to ask the gift giver to donate my gift?
Not if you ask kindly and privately. Most givers would rather their gift find a good home than gather dust. Sending it to someone who loved it at the reveal — an Aunt Edna type — is the warmest version of the move.
Can I ask for money instead of a white elephant gift?
Only for un-ordered retailer gifts, and only gently: 'Hey, Venmo me and I'll buy it here' keeps the budget identical and lets the recipient pick the variant they actually want. Never demand cash for an already-shipped gift — donate the item or regift instead.
How do I regift a white elephant gift without being rude?
Follow the Legend Returns Clause: re-wrap it well, store it with the holiday decorations, and redeploy it next year — ideally to a different household so the story keeps traveling. The best regifts become family legends.
Does someone always end up unhappy with their gift?
Almost every game has one person who wishes they weren't stuck with Uncle Randall's Dollar Store find from 2016. The Three-Owner Rule caps the damage, the final swap gives Player 1 a fix, and the gracious fixes above handle the rest.
## More rules, fewer duds
The full FAQ covers 25 other disputes, and the gift ideas list helps you avoid giving next year’s Uncle Randall moment.
Read the full FAQ →

Title: White Elephant vs Secret Santa vs Grab Bag

Quick answer
White elephant lets players steal gifts live, with the taker choosing; Secret Santa assigns each person a recipient in advance, and the secret giver chooses. Both use a published budget cap, but Secret Santa also needs a name list. This page compares them with grab bag, ornament exchange, and Dirty Santa.
The one-line version: Secret Santa assigns gifts to people in advance; a grab bag assigns them by luck; a white elephant lets everyone fight over them live. Same budget, wildly different evenings.
## The comparison table
Six minutes of setup versus a whole evening of chaos.

## When to pick each one
Honest recommendations, not rivalry.
### Choose white elephant when…
PICK ME
You have 8+ players, a shared sense of humor, and a group that enjoys light betrayal. The steal chain is the entertainment.
The game is the show: draws, steals, locks, and the final swap. Rulebook and the 22 names for it are one click away.
### Choose Secret Santa when…
THOUGHTFUL
People care about getting something they’ll actually use, or the group includes folks who’d hate public stealing.
The assignment does the work: each person buys for one named colleague with a wishlist. Thoughtful, low-drama, and it scales to offices — just not to chaos.
### Choose a grab bag when…
QUICK
You need a 10-minute filler with zero prep — kids’ parties, raffle nights, the lull before the reveal.
Numbered tickets, numbered gifts, done. It’s the exchange equivalent of a coin flip — fair, fast, forgettable.
## The mix-and-match move
What the savviest hosts actually do.
Run a Yankee Swap (that’s white elephant with a formal final swap), or start the office with Secret Santa and finish the holiday party with a white elephant — thoughtful gifting first, chaos for dessert. Dirty Santa is the same game with a different accent; the names page settles the vocabulary.
## White Elephant vs Secret Santa — FAQ
The questions this page always raises.
What is the difference between white elephant and Secret Santa?
Secret Santa assigns each person a named recipient in advance and gifts are given, never stolen. White elephant has a shared pile, numbered turns, and live stealing under the Three-Owner Rule — the drama is the point.
Is Yankee Swap the same as white elephant?
Functionally yes — different regions use different names. 'Yankee Swap' usually implies the formal final-swap for Player 1; 'white elephant' and 'Dirty Santa' are regional labels for the same steal-chain game.
Which gift exchange is best for large groups?
White elephant for entertainment (up to 40 in Party tier, 150 in Business), grab bag for speed, Secret Santa when personalization matters more than spectacle.
Can you play both at the same party?
Yes — a common office pattern is Secret Santa for thoughtful gifts at dinner and a white elephant for the after-dinner chaos. Budget-separate them so nobody double-spends.

## Why $10 gifts steal anyway
The cheap-gift paradox.
Steal appeal isn’t price — it’s universality plus a story. A tiny cassette dispenser out-steals a $40 gadget because everyone understands it instantly and everyone knows who it should live with. ## White Elephant Gifts Under $10 — FAQ

What is a good white elephant gift under $10?

Can a $10 gift win a white elephant?
Yes — cheap-but-perfect gifts steal constantly because everyone wants them and nobody feels bad taking one. Universality beats price in steal appeal.
Where do I buy white elephant gifts last minute?
Walmart, Target, and Amazon all filter under-$10; every button above opens a live search or product page. For a truly same-night game, the paste-a-link feature lets players add gifts straight from a retailer page.
What should I not buy under $10?
Consumables that expire fast, anything needing batteries you didn’t include, and the regift that still has last year’s tag. Cheap is a budget; cheap looking is a choice.

Title: Classroom White Elephant: Kid-Friendly Rules

Quick answer
Classic white elephant stealing can turn a classroom into a courtroom, so this page offers three classroom-safe variants by grade level: a no-steal swap for K–4, steal-with-permission for grades 3–6, and a game-show steal for grade 5 and up, where a correct trivia answer earns the steal. Everyone keeps a gift.
Golden rule of the classroom edition: nobody loses what they already opened. Young kids process a steal as a personal loss — so the variants below either remove stealing, gate it behind permission, or turn it into a game-show moment where everyone still wins.
## Three classroom-safe variants
Pick by grade level. All three end with everyone keeping something.
### No-Steal Swap (K–4)
VARIANT 1
The purest version: unwrap, admire, pass to the next person to admire, keep. The suspense does all the work.
Players unwrap in number order and simply keep what they get — the drama is the mystery, not the theft. Works as a book exchange: every kid brings a wrapped book, leaves with a new one. Zero tears, maximum reading list.
### Steal-With-Permission (3–6)
VARIANT 2
A steal is only legal if the current holder nods. Consent-based stealing sounds quaint; it teaches negotiation and keeps the energy.
Stealing is allowed, but the holder can say no once per turn — teaching kids to ask, persuade, and accept an answer. Cap it at one steal per gift so the pile keeps moving, and let the teacher be the Three-Owner Rule (they count aloud — it works).
### Game-Show Steal (5–grade+)
VARIANT 3
Steals must be earned: answer a trivia question (or tell the joke from the winter concert) and the steal is legal. Chaos with a curriculum.
The teacher keeps a stack of grade-level questions; a correct answer buys the steal. Wrong answer = unwrap instead. It gamifies the steal so well that middle-schoolers forget to be too cool for it.
## Teacher-approved gift rules
The five filters that keep the office call home happy.
- Budget: $5–$10 max — and say so in the note home, with the date two weeks out so nobody scrambles.
- No food with allergens — check the class list first; packaged-and-labeled only, or skip food entirely.
- Gender-neutral and grade-level — the gift should fit any kid in the room. Think books, art supplies, desk toys, puzzles.
- No passwords, accounts, or screens — physical gifts only, nothing that needs a download to work.
- Wrapped anonymously — and no peeking-then-rejecting; that's the muscle the no-steal variant builds.
The age-groups guide maps gift styles to tiers, and the under-$10 list doubles as a class budget list.
## Running it with the app (yes, in class)
For grades 5+, or the staff party.
The free tier (up to 8 players) handles a small group; a class of 24 fits the Party tier. Use the app to draw the order — it ends the who-goes-first debate forever — and display the pile on the projector. For class parties, the no-steal variant needs none of the enforcement features; for the staff holiday party, run the full rulebook with the MC tools and let a teacher finally win something.
## Classroom White Elephant — FAQ
The questions this page always raises.
How do you play white elephant with kids?
Use the no-steal variant: kids unwrap in numbered order and keep what they get, so the mystery supplies the fun. Older grades can graduate to steal-with-permission or game-show steals.
What is a good classroom gift exchange budget?
$5–$10 per gift, announced in a note home at least two weeks ahead. Books, art supplies, and desk toys are the safe, gender-neutral, allergen-free picks.
How does a classroom book exchange work?
Each student brings a wrapped book in good condition; kids unwrap in number order and keep the book they reveal. It runs exactly like a no-steal white elephant — same suspense, zero tears, and everyone goes home reading.
Is stealing too mean for young kids?
Often, yes — kids process a steal as losing something that was theirs. Keep it kind: no-steal for K–4, permission-based stealing for grades 3–6, and full rules once they can lose with grace (most can by middle school).

Title: White Elephant Invitation Wording: 9 Free Templates

Quick answer
A good white elephant invitation states the date, time, place, budget, and the basic rules so guests don't text you questions all week. This page gives nine ready-to-use templates, including family, office, funny, classroom, async, and premium versions, plus subject lines and a details checklist.
Every template below is copy-paste ready: swap the [BRACKETS], keep the rules line (it prevents 90% of day-of questions), and send. Rule Sheet handouts for printing, email, and text live one click away in the resources.
## The templates
Seven invites + two subject lines + one checklist.
### The classic family one
FAMILY
One line of logistics, one line of rules, one line of warning.
You’re invited to the [FAMILY NAME] White Elephant! [DATE] at [TIME], [ADDRESS]. Bring one wrapped gift, around $[AMOUNT]. Rules are simple: three owners and it locks, no steal-backs, Player 1 gets the final swap. The app tracks everything — join at [EVENT LINK]. Last year’s champ, prepare to be dethroned.
### The office one
OFFICE
HR-friendly, calendar-ready, zero ambiguity about the cap.
Our team’s White Elephant is [DATE] at [TIME] in [LOCATION / VIDEO LINK]. Budget: $[AMOUNT] — firm, per policy and per tradition. Async-friendly: turns land in your inbox, steal on your own schedule all week. Join: [EVENT LINK]. Questions? The rulebook: stolenelephants.com/white-elephant-rules
### The funny one
FUNNY
For groups that choose their gift exchange by how hard they can laugh.
🐘 WHITE ELEPHANT: [DATE], [TIME], [PLACE]. Bring a $[AMOUNT] gift you’ll pretend you didn’t buy yourself. Three owners and it locks. No crying (out loud). Uncle Randall’s 2016 masterpiece is eligible to return. Join: [EVENT LINK]
### The classroom one
CLASSROOM
Goes home in a backpack; survives a parent’s second read.
Dear families — on [DATE], our class will hold a Book Exchange! Each student brings one wrapped book in good condition (new or like-new). We’ll unwrap together in class and everyone takes home a “new” book. Please keep it under $10 and avoid food items. Note by [DATE] if you’d like a book provided instead.
### The virtual / async one
VIRTUAL
For teams across time zones — the game fits the week, not the calendar.
Our White Elephant is async this year: [START DAY] to [END DAY]. One gift, $[AMOUNT], one link — join at [EVENT LINK] and take your turn when your workday allows. Hospital beds, airports, and other time zones are all first-class players here. Finale chain: [OPTIONAL VIDEO CALL, DAY/TIME].
### The premium one
PREMIUM
For the night you’re all feeling generous — or rich, or both.
You’re cordially invited to a Premium White Elephant: [DATE], [TIME], [ADDRESS]. This year’s cap is $[AMOUNT] — think French presses, not fingernail clippers. Same rules, finer prizes. Dress code: better than last year. Join: [EVENT LINK]
### The day-of reminder text
REMINDER
Two hours out. Works for any of the above.
⏰ Tonight: white elephant at [TIME], [PLACE]. Bring your $[AMOUNT] gift. Numbers drawn at [TIME] sharp — late = last pick. Rules refresher: stolenelephants.com/white-elephant-rules
### Email subject lines that get opened
SUBJECTS
🐘 You’re invited: [FAMILY/TEAM] White Elephant — [DATE] Bring one gift, leave with a better one (White Elephant, [DATE]) The steal chain begins [DATE] — join the White Elephant Reminder: White Elephant [TONIGHT/TOMORROW] — $[AMOUNT], one wrapped gift
## What every invite needs
The five details that prevent the 9 p.m. panic text.
- Date, time, place — or the async window start/end, if the game runs all week.
- The price cap, stated as firm — '$25' invites interpretation; 'cap: $25, firm' doesn't.
- One wrapped gift — say 'wrapped'; someone will otherwise bring a gift bag with a bow on it and a receipt inside.
- The rules line or a link — 'three owners and it locks; no steal-backs; final swap for Player 1' or just link the rulebook.
- The event link — join before the party, not during the draw.
## White Elephant Invitation Wording — FAQ
The questions this page always raises.
What should a white elephant invitation say?
Date, time, place, the firm price cap, 'one wrapped gift', the event link, and one line of rules ('three owners and it locks'). Everything else is decoration.
How far in advance should you send white elephant invites?
Two to three weeks for family and office games — enough shopping runway without the invite getting buried. A reminder text the day of rescues the rest.
How do you word a virtual white elephant invitation?
State the async window instead of a single time (‘play anytime between Monday and Thursday’), the cap, and the join link. Add the finale call time if you’re booking one.
What is a fun white elephant invite?
Name the tradition (‘Uncle Randall’s 2016 masterpiece is eligible to return’), warn about the lock rule, and keep the logistics to three lines. The funny template above does all three.

Title: Stolen Elephants Pricing: Free, Party & Business Plans

Quick answer
Stolen Elephants charges per event, never per seat or per month. The Free plan covers up to 8 players for $0, Party is $19 per event for up to 40 players, and Business is $99 per event for up to 150 players. All plans include the rulebook engine, which handles draws, steals, Three-Owner locks, and the final swap.

## Which tier fits your group?
Three honest recommendations.
### Free — up to 8 players
Perfect for: family game night, one classroom, a squad of friends. The entire rulebook engine, zero dollars.
Full draw, steal chains, Three-Owner Rule locks, final swap — live or async. If your circle fits around one table, you’ll never need to pay.
### Party — 9 to 40 players
Perfect for: office teams, big family reunions, club holiday parties. One flat $19 covers everyone.
Everything in Free, sized for the whole department: async across the week, spectator-plus for remote guests, and the finale chain as the group event it deserves to be.
### Business — 41 to 150 players
Perfect for: whole-company holiday chaos, multi-office events, the all-hands that needs a scoreboard.
Same engine, company scale. One event link, every office and time zone in one pile, and no per-seat math when the headcount wobbles between November and December.
## Common pricing questions
Short answers; the FAQ has more.
Is it per person? No — per event. A 40-player Party event costs $19 total, not $19 a head.
Is there a subscription? No. Pay when you host an event; play free under 8 players forever.
Can we upgrade after we’ve started setting up? Yes. Until the game starts, the host can upgrade from inside the game, pay for the new tier by card, and invite the rest of the floor. Once the game starts, the plan is locked in.
## Stolen Elephants Pricing — FAQ
The questions this page always raises.
How much does Stolen Elephants cost?
Free for up to 8 players. Party tier is $19 per event for 9–40 players, and Business tier is $99 per event for 41–150 players. Always per event — never per person or per month.
Is there a free plan?
Yes — the full rulebook engine (draw, steals, Three-Owner Rule locks, final swap, live or async) is free for groups up to 8 players, with no time limit.
What’s the difference between Party and Business tiers?
Party covers 9–40 players at $19 per event, Business covers 41–150 at $99. Both include a custom logo on your event and gift and thank-you videos; Business allows longer videos (45 seconds instead of 30).
